summary: This document defines a new Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for hardware device identifiers. It gives sensor data streams, storage systems and equipment inventories a general way to write down a device's identity as a URN. That representation can then be passed along between applications that need to know which device is meant.

eli5.summary: Every gadget needs a name tag that anyone can read the same way. This document invents a standard style of name tag for hardware, so different programs can talk about the same gadget without mixing it up.

questions: how to represent hardware device identity as a urn
how to write a 1-wire device id as a urn
urn dev os and ops subtypes
subtitle: A URN namespace, urn:dev, for writing down hardware device identifiers such as MAC addresses and 1-Wire IDs in a uniform way.

tldr.problem: Sensor data streams, inventories and similar systems need to say which device they mean, but there was no general URN type for identifiers such as MAC addresses or 1-Wire IDs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9039 registers the URN namespace "dev" with subtypes (mac, ow, org, os, ops) that wrap an existing device identifier in an ASCII string like urn:dev:ow:10e2073a01080063.
tldr.outcome: Applications can pass a self-describing device identity in any field that carries URNs, such as JSON or SenML, without agreeing on how to read raw octets. The RFC also warns that long-lived identifiers raise privacy concerns.

facts.label: Subtypes defined
facts.value: mac, ow, org, os, ops, plus example

today: RFC 9039 is a Proposed Standard (June 2021). No RFC obsoleting or updating it is recorded in the metadata for this site, so it is the definition of the urn:dev namespace.

sections.title: Why a Device URN
sections.content:
RFC 9039 describes a new Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for hardware device identifiers. A general representation of device identity is useful in sensor data streams and storage and in equipment inventories. A URN can be carried in protocols built to carry URNs and stored in formats such as XML, JSON or SenML.

Using URNs is often preferable because they are universally recognized and self-describing. Nobody has to agree beforehand that an octet string is, for instance, a MAC address. The cost is some extra bytes compared with, for instance, a 4-byte binary IPv4 address.

The namespace covers cases where no convenient URN type already exists. Identifiers that already have their own URN types, such as IMEI (RFC 7254) and MEID (RFC 8464), should keep using them. UUID URNs (RFC 4122) are another option and are often preferred for general-purpose uses, while the device URNs are recommended for constrained environments.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone writing a gadget's number in their own way, this gives one standard label that says what kind of number it is. Labels for phones already exist, so those keep using theirs.

sections.title: Syntax of a DEV URN
sections.content:
The namespace identifier is dev, version 1. A DEV URN is written in ASCII characters as urn:dev:, then a subtype and its identifier, then optional components. The grammar is given in ABNF.

Each body starts with a subtype name such as mac: or ow:. Except for the MAC address and 1-Wire subtypes, a DEV URN may also contain optional colon-separated identifiers for extensibility. At the end, optional underscore-separated components describe individual aspects of a device. Their strings and meaning are up to the device designers, and they could refer to specific interfaces or functions within the device.

DEV URNs do not use r-, q- or f-components. The RFC does not deviate from the general URN syntax and normalization rules of RFC 8141, and it considers percent-encoding undesirable in DEV URNs because of SenML naming rules.

Two DEV URNs are URN-equivalent when their assigned-name portions are octet-by-octet equal after case normalization of the scheme and namespace identifier. The rest of the URN is compared case-sensitively. To make comparison easier, implementations are RECOMMENDED to use lowercase letters wherever they have a choice.
sections.eli5: A device label always starts with the same opening words, then says what kind of number follows, then the number itself. Capital letters count as different letters, so everyone should use small letters to be safe.

sections.title: Purpose, Assignment and Resolution
sections.content:
DEV URNs identify devices using device-specific identifiers such as network card hardware addresses. They are scoped to be globally applicable. Typical uses include equipment inventories and smart object systems, and tasks from discovery to intrusion detection and simple catalogues of system information.

The URN does not manage identifier assignment. How an identifier is assigned depends on the subtype, and conflicts caused by local or algorithmic assignment are not something DEV URNs handle; they simply refer to a particular identifier. A single device may have several identifiers, for example one for each link technology it supports. The DEV URN type SHOULD only be used for hardware-based identifiers that are expected to be persistent.

Device identifiers are not expected to be globally resolvable, and no identifier resolution system is expected. Systems may match identifiers locally against previously seen identifiers or configured information.
sections.eli5: The label only copies the number that the gadget already has. It does not hand out numbers and it is not a phone book for finding the gadget.

sections.title: The DEV URN Subtypes
sections.content:
The RFC defines five subtypes and reserves a sixth for examples.

  • mac: the full EUI-64 identifier as a hexadecimal string, always exactly 16 characters. A MAC-48 or EUI-48 address is converted by keeping the first three octets, inserting 0xffff (MAC-48) or 0xfffe (EUI-48) as the fourth and fifth octets, and keeping the last three octets. Assignment rests with the IEEE Registration Authority.
  • ow: a 1-Wire device ID, a 64-bit identifier made of an 8-bit family code, a 48-bit identifier unique within the family and an 8-bit CRC. It is written as 16 hexadecimal characters, the last two being the CRC, which implementations MAY check.
  • org: identifiers meaningful only within an organization, identified by its Private Enterprise Number (PEN). The number cannot be zero or have leading zeroes.
  • os: a PEN plus a serial number defined by the organization.
  • ops: a PEN, a product class and a serial number, both defined by the organization.
  • example: reserved for use in examples.

The os and ops subtypes were originally defined in the Open Mobile Alliance Lightweight Machine to Machine standard and are collected here. The os syntax was changed to avoid characters not allowed in the SenML Name field. Where randomized MAC addresses are used, the resulting DEV URNs cannot be expected to be unique.
sections.eli5: There are a few kinds of labels. One is for the number printed on a network card, one for a tiny sensor chip, and others for numbers a company makes up itself. Each kind has its own short name after the opening words.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a table of sample URNs. urn:dev:mac:0024beffff804ff1 is the MAC-48 address 0024be804ff1 converted to EUI-64 format, while urn:dev:mac:0024befffe804ff1 is the same bytes treated as an EUI-48 address. urn:dev:ow:10e2073a01080063 is a 1-Wire temperature sensor, and urn:dev:ow:264437f5000000ed_humidity names the humidity part of a multi-sensor device using an underscore component.

For the organization subtypes it uses the example organization 32473 from RFC 5612: urn:dev:org:32473-foo, urn:dev:os:32473-123456 and urn:dev:ops:32473-Refrigerator-5002. A DEV URN can appear in SenML data, where it names the source of a measurement.
sections.eli5: Here are sample labels: one for a network card, one for a temperature chip, and one for fridge number 5002 from a pretend company.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
An implementation MUST preserve the limits and behaviors the device identifiers already have. An identifier that is meant to be immutable must not become mutable just because it is wrapped in a DEV URN, and the RFC does not override what the underlying device specifications say.

DEV URNs often represent long-term stable unique identifiers. These can enable correlating information about a specific device over a long period, location tracking and device-specific vulnerability exploitation (RFC 7721). In some systems the identifier cannot easily be changed, so leaking identifiers outside the system meant to use them should be avoided.

Systems should also expect devices to report incorrect identifiers, accidentally or maliciously, and illegitimate parties to manipulate identifiers in transit. Integrity protection, trusted devices and management practices help. As with RFC 4122, the RFC says not to assume DEV URNs are hard to guess.
sections.eli5: A gadget's number never changes, so anyone who sees it can recognize that gadget again and again. Keep it private, and do not trust a number just because someone says it.

sections.title: IANA Registration and New Subtypes
sections.content:
IANA has registered the URN namespace dev and created a "DEV URN Subtypes" registry under "Device Identification". The initial entries are mac, ow, org, os, ops and example.

New subtypes can be added through Specification Required or IESG Approval (RFC 8126). These are appropriate when a new namespace of device identifier is defined in a stable fashion and has a publicly available specification. The RFC prefers that a broadly used, long-term identifier be registered with the IETF rather than used through the org subtype, though org can serve as a temporary measure.
sections.eli5: A keeper of lists has written down the label kinds. A new kind can be added if it has a clear public description.
